content: The references provided are a collection of studies, reports, and systematic reviews related to tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and associated challenges, particularly in populations affected by HIV, children, and other vulnerable groups. 1. Ahmad Khan et al. (2014) evaluated the effectiveness of symptom-based TB screening among people living with HIV. The study concluded that the performance of such screening methods was suboptimal, highlighting the need for improved diagnostic strategies. 2. Calnan (2016) discussed strategies for TB screening in HIV-infected and uninfected pregnant and postpartum women in Swaziland, presented at the 47th World Conference on Lung Health. The study emphasized the importance of tailored approaches for these populations. 3. Hanifa et al. (2015) assessed the WHO 4-symptom screening tool to rule out TB using data from the XPHACTOR study. The findings suggested limitations in the tool's ability to exclude TB, necessitating further refinement. 4. Kufa et al. (2012) investigated undiagnosed TB among HIV clinic attendees and its association with antiretroviral therapy. The study underscored the implications for intensified case finding, isoniazid preventive therapy, and infection control measures. 5. LaCourse et al. (2016) examined TB case finding in HIV-infected pregnant women in Kenya. The study revealed poor performance of symptom screening and rapid diagnostic tests, indicating the need for better diagnostic tools. 6. Nguyen et al. (2016) evaluated the yield of chest radiography in TB screening for HIV-infected individuals at a district-level clinic. The study highlighted the utility of radiography in improving TB detection rates. 7. Rangaka et al. (2014) conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to assess the efficacy of isoniazid plus antiretroviral therapy in preventing TB. The results demonstrated the potential benefits of this combination therapy. 8. Den Boon et al. (2006) evaluated the use of symptom and chest radiographic screening in TB prevalence surveys. The study highlighted the complementary role of radiography in identifying TB cases. 9. Adetifa et al. (2016) reported on a nationwide TB prevalence survey in Gambia, providing critical epidemiological data to inform TB control strategies. 10. Ayles et al. (2009) investigated the prevalence of TB, HIV, and respiratory symptoms in two Zambian communities. The findings emphasized the need for integrated TB and HIV control efforts. 11. Corbett et al. (2010) assessed the diagnostic value of provider-initiated symptom screening for TB in Zimbabwe and the effect of HIV status on screening outcomes. The study highlighted the challenges of TB diagnosis in high HIV prevalence settings. 12. Van’t Hoog et al. (2012) explored screening strategies for TB prevalence surveys, emphasizing the value of combining chest radiography with symptom screening. 13. Datta et al. (2001) conducted a TB survey in a tribal population in North Arcot District, India, providing insights into TB prevalence in underserved communities. 14. Gopi et al. (2003) performed a baseline survey of TB prevalence in a South Indian community at the start of a DOTS program, offering valuable data for program evaluation. 15. Kapata et al. (2016) presented results from Zambia's first national TB prevalence survey, highlighting the burden of TB and informing national control efforts. 16. The Ministry of Health in Cambodia (2002, 2010) published reports on national TB prevalence surveys, providing critical data for TB control planning. 17. Senkoro et al. (2016) reported on the prevalence of pulmonary TB in Tanzania's adult population, based on a national survey conducted in 2012. 18. Kebede et al. (2014) described Ethiopia's first population-based national TB prevalence survey, conducted in 2010–2011, which provided foundational data for TB control. 19. Law et al. (2015) reported on the first national TB prevalence survey in Lao PDR, conducted in 2010–2011, highlighting the burden of TB in the region. 20. Auguste et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review and economic evaluation of latent TB diagnosis in children, immunocompromised individuals, and recent arrivals from high TB incidence countries. 21. Mahomed et al. (2011) compared the tuberculin skin test and QuantiFERON-TB Gold in predicting TB disease in South African adolescents, providing insights into diagnostic accuracy. 22. Mathad et al. (2016) investigated immune responses associated with latent TB test discordance in HIV-infected pregnant women, contributing to understanding of TB immunology. 23. McCarthy et al. (2015) highlighted the high incidence of latent TB infection among South African healthcare workers, calling for urgent action to protect this vulnerable group. 24. Rangaka et al. (2014) conducted a trial on isoniazid plus antiretroviral therapy to prevent TB, demonstrating its efficacy in reducing TB incidence. 25. Sharma et al. (2017) compared the tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assays in diagnosing latent TB infection in high TB burden settings, providing evidence for diagnostic decision-making. 26. Alsdurf et al. (2016) reviewed the cascade of care in latent TB diagnosis and treatment, identifying gaps and opportunities for improvement. 27. Swindells et al. (2019) evaluated a one-month regimen of rifapentine plus isoniazid to prevent HIV-related TB, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for programmatic implementation. 28. Hamada et al. (2017) compared a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid with daily isoniazid monotherapy for latent TB treatment, providing evidence for shorter regimens. 29. Stagg et al. (2014) conducted a network meta-analysis on latent TB treatment, comparing various regimens and their effectiveness. 30. Shepardson and MacKenzie (2014) updated the cost-effectiveness of a 12-dose regimen for latent TB infection, considering new rifapentine prices. 31. Martins et al. (2011) evaluated new regimens to prevent TB in adults with HIV infection, providing evidence for shorter, effective preventive treatments. 32. Sterling et al. (2016) assessed a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine and isoniazid for treating latent TB infection in HIV-coinfected individuals, demonstrating its efficacy. 33. Villarino et al. (2015) conducted a trial on a three-month, 12-dose regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for preventing TB in children and adolescents, showing promising results. 34. The Global Tuberculosis Report (2023) provided a comprehensive overview of the global TB burden, progress, and challenges in TB control. 35. Takizawa et al. (1999) studied the comparative arthropathy of fluoroquinolones in dogs, contributing to understanding of drug safety. 36. Hampel et al. (1997) reviewed the worldwide clinical experience of ciprofloxacin in pediatrics, focusing on safety and compassionate use. 37. Warren (1997) discussed rheumatologic aspects of pediatric cystic fibrosis patients treated with fluoroquinolones, highlighting potential side effects. 38. The FDA issued safety announcements reinforcing the risks of serious low blood sugar levels and mental health side effects associated with fluoroquinolone antibiotics, requiring label changes. 39. Acar et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on pregnancy outcomes following quinolone and fluoroquinolone exposure, providing evidence for risk assessment. 40. The WHO consolidated guidelines on TB preventive treatment (second edition) summarized evidence and recommendations for TB prevention, including the use of levofloxacin in children exposed to multidrug-resistant TB. 41. The TB CHAMP and V-QUIN trials evaluated the efficacy and safety of levofloxacin for preventing TB in child contacts of MDR-TB patients, providing critical data for preventive therapy strategies. These studies collectively highlight the complexities of TB diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, particularly in high-risk populations, and underscore the need for continued research and innovation in TB control.
